newsitem.title: THAILAND: New crackdown signals business as usual in Burma.
newsitem.headline: New crackdown signals business as usual in Burma.

text.p: The latest wave of arrests of Burmese pro-democracy politicians shows it's business as usual in Rangoon despite global pressures to ease the military government's authoritarian rule, diplomats said on Thursday.

News of the arrests of at least 60 members of opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) this week ahead of a party gathering show Burma's generals are determined to keep total control, Rangoon-based diplomats said.

The United States officially imposed economic sanctions on Burma this week, banning all new U.S. investment as a public condemnation of the military regime's human rights abuses and its repression of the democracy movement led by Suu Kyi.
Burma was also awaiting word on its entry as a full member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). It was expected to join along with Cambodia and Laos later this year.
Foreign ministers of ASEAN, which groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam, were due to meet on May 31 to discuss the matter.
The United States and other nations have urged ASEAN not to admit Burma because of its political and human rights record.
But analysts say neither sanctions nor ASEAN are uppermost on the minds of the State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC). Suu Kyi is.

Ever since the SLORC freed the Nobel Peace laureate from six years house arrest in July 1995, one of its key aims has been to control and contain her and the NLD, which represent the biggest threat to its total control, analysts and diplomats said.

"My understanding is that it is more important for the SLORC to keep security and to deal with the NLD than anything else," one Asian diplomat said. "Their priority is to keep security, not become an ASEAN member."
He and others said the SLORC likely feared the NLD might issue strong statements at a planned May 27 party celebration to commemorate the party's landslide 1990 election victory.
The SLORC never recognised the results of the poll and has cracked down on elected MPs and top NLD organisers ever since.
"What this means is, they don't want the meeting to go ahead and they're taking measures to stop it," another diplomat said about the latest wave of arrests.

Last May, the NLD held a much-publicised meeting on the election anniversary that the government tried to stop. Although the SLORC arrested 261 senior NLD members, most of whom were MPs elected in 1990, Suu Kyi and the NLD held the meeting anyway.
Suu Kyi said afterwards the party had vowed to push forward to bring democracy to Burma. Among other things she said the NLD planned to write was an alternative constitution for Burma.
Suu Kyi pulled the NLD out of the National Convention that is drafting guidelines for a new constitution because she said the hand-picked group did not represent the will of the people.
The government saw the announcement as a direct affront to its leadership, and diplomats said they might fear the NLD will unveil its draft constitution at the upcoming May 27 meeting.
"The SLORC is very afraid the NLD will announce their draft constitution," the Asian diplomat said. "I don't know if they will allow them to have the meeting."

The government has not confirmed or denied reports of the 60 arrests, but said on Thursday that the NLD was trying to create problems in the country and it had taken necessary measures to ensure peace.
Diplomats said the arrests of the NLD members, most of whom were coming to Rangoon from the provinces, were not unexpected.
"We heard last week that MPs were being notified to pack their toothbrushes and be ready," one diplomat said.
Suu Kyi has repeatedly said she and all the NLD members accept arrest as a way of life.
More than 2,000 NLD members and supporters were detained last year. Although many were released, some were charged and sentenced to long prison terms.
